Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

vignette: At fifty, divorced and living alone in a quiet apartment, Kiet sat in the dimly lit green room of a downtown theater, his fingers tracing the worn fretboard of his acoustic guitar. He had stopped performing in unfamiliar venues months ago, unable to assess the danger when he could not map the exits or calculate the blind spots where a figure might emerge. The stalking campaign that began five years ago had shattered his spatial safety. He remembered the man’s voice echoing through his walls, the shadow pacing his street long after midnight, and the hollow thud of the police filing a report and closing the case without ever visiting his door. That institutional failure had become a quiet earthquake in his chest. He had come to believe he was a weak person, a man who could not shield himself even when authorities refused to look, and over time, the grief of that powerlessness calcified into a heavy emotional numbness. This collapse of self-competence directly shaped how his mind retained the trauma. Because he viewed himself as fundamentally helpless and the justice system as indifferent, his brain latched onto the past as a site of unresolved danger. Parts of the event remained entirely blank, memory gaps that haunted him no matter how hard he tried to recall them, while other fragments appeared suddenly without warning and then vanished. The full sensory reliving of these moments felt completely real across all his senses at once, a visceral proof that he was failing to process his own life. Each intrusive reliving actively reinforced his negative appraisals; the more hollow and inadequate he felt, the more violently the memories demanded his attention, pulling him backward into the exact moments where his control had dissolved. His daily routine as a session musician became a landscape of constant scanning. Before entering a studio, he would spend twenty minutes watching the other players and clients for signs that they might harm him, his eyes darting to hands, shoulders, and doorways. The sheer exhaustion of this threat monitoring, compounded by his refusal to venture beyond his familiar neighborhood, left him emotionally drained and cemented his conviction that the institutions meant to protect people had simply let him fall. His hypervigilant scanning actively triggered the fragmented memories, as a sudden glimpse of a similar jacket or the sound of heavy footsteps would flood his system with unbidden pieces of the stalker’s approach. The sensory reliving, once summoned by his environment, pushed him deeper into heightened threat assessment, making him scan every new room for danger. This cycle tightened over the subsequent months. His negative appraisals of weakness and systemic abandonment directly fueled his threat monitoring, as he interpreted neutral streetlights and passing cars as deliberate surveillance. The memory fragments, once triggered, would spiral back into his core beliefs, convincing him that his emotional numbness was a permanent sentence rather than a temporary survival strategy. He found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, lying awake while his pulse drummed against his ribs, certain that the threat was still mapping his route. The loop was inescapable: the more he watched others and avoided unknown spaces, the more his brain stored danger cues, and the more those cues convinced him he was broken. He finally walked into the clinic because his hands had begun to tremble during tuning, a failure that threatened his livelihood, and because he was terrified that the numbness would become permanent, leaving him entirely alone with the ghosts he could neither remember nor outrun.
